newsitem.title: UK: Car makers, consumers collide over new crash tests.
newsitem.headline: Car makers, consumers collide over new crash tests.

text.p: European car industry groups and consumer bodies on Tuesday collided head-on over new independent crash test results for Europe's top-selling small cars.

The European New Car Assessment Programme (Euro-NCAP), sponsored by Britain's Department of Transport and European consumer groups, showed Ford's Fiesta and Volkswagen's Polo came out best in the crash tests. Rover Group's Rover 100 model was bottom of the seven-car league.

The Euro-NCAP tests go beyond existing requirements -- which examine only frontal impact -- by assessing front and side impacts and the effect on pedestrians. The front impact test also is conducted at 40 mph (64 kph), faster than the existing manufacturers' type approval test at 31 mph (50 kph).

Consumer groups and British Road Safety Minister John Bowis hailed the launch of the independent test results, saying they would raise public awareness and spur car manufacturers to incorporate more safety features.

"Motorists have the right to know how their car would perform if it came to the crunch. These results should make motorists choose safety," Neil Johnson, chief executive of Britain's RAC motoring organisation said in a statement.

But Britain's Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) and ACEA, the European Automobile Manufacturers Association, said the tests were flawed and consumers could be misled by what they called the limited scope of the programme.

"Although the models selected may be among the most popular, the vehicle with the best rating may not be the safest car in this sector and the car with the lowest rating will almost certainly not be the least safe," they said.
Of a possible five stars, the Fiesta and Polo gained three. Fiat's Punto, Nissan's Micra, Renault's Clio and Vauxhall's Corsa won two. The Rover 100 won only one star.

Roger King, SMMT communications director, said the primary flaw in the tests was the higher speed used in the offset frontal impact test, set at 64 kph. King said more than 95 percent of frontal impacts occurred at speeds below 56 kph.

"In terms of force...this is a massive increase. To engineer a super mini car to pass this test at such a speed might require stiffer front ends which will then perform more aggressively in collision with the side or rear of another car," King said.
"They are testing to a far higher impact speed than we are obliged to design the cars to," he said.

SMMT and ACEA said the tests also failed to take into account many safety features such as anti-locking brakes or passenger airbags which were omitted from some test cars to ensure consistency with models equipped with them.

They said only two cars and one variant per model of car were considered and said different numbers of doors or different engines could affect crash performance, a view echoed by Rover Group, a division of German luxury car maker BMW.
"Rover has reservations over publication of these results which will distort the market...the belief that more stars equals more safety is untenable," Rover said in a statement.
It said Department of Transport data from a study of over 170,000 real car accidents showed the Rover 100 was in line with the average of other small cars in the safety stakes.
At stake is the hotly-fought-for small car market.

The SMMT said so-called superminis accounted for just over a quarter of the 2.25 million new cars bought annually in Britain, with small to medium size cars such as Ford's Escort taking a third. Supermini sales grew by 4.4 percent last year, outstripping average market growth of 4.1 percent.
